Evidence suggests that the introduction of legislation limiting the number of tablets sold in a single transaction in the UK in 1998 led to a reduction in the number of tablets taken in overdose cases. However, some authors have disputed this finding (Hawton 2001; Morgan 2007). 2. Pesticide ingestion is responsible for an estimated 370,000 suicides annually worldwide, with a disproportionate number occurring in lowand middle-income countries (WHO 2009). 3. Access to pesticides can be restricted by limiting their sales and providing safer storage options. 4. Many high-income countries have already banned the use and export of the most lethal pesticides. Evidence from countries such as Jordan and Samoa indicates that such bans are associated with a subsequent reduction in suicide rates (WHO 2009). 5. Safer pesticide storage, particularly in developing countries, can be achieved by providing locked storage boxes, encouraging centralized and communal storage, and educating pesticide users about the risks associated with their use, as well as safe storage and disposal practices. 6. Hanging is the most common method of suicide worldwide (Gunnell 2005). 7. Restricting access to means of hanging is often not feasible at the general population level because commonly used ligatures and ligature points are universally available (Sarchiapone 2011). 8. In controlled environments such as hospitals and prisons, access to means of hanging can be restricted by introducing safer (ligature-free) cells, ligature-free bedding and clothing for high-risk individuals, and collapsible ligature points such as shower rails (Gunnell 2005). 9. Among males, the proportion of suicides involving firearms ranges from 0.2% in Japan to 60.6% in the United States (WHO 2009). 10. Reducing access to firearms can be achieved through legislation, enforcement, amnesties, and collection schemes. 11. Legislative measures to reduce firearm access may include banning certain types of firearms, implementing licensing and registration schemes for suppliers and owners, enforcing minimum waiting periods between licensing and purchasing, conducting safe storage checks, and performing background checks and/or psychological testing for prospective buyers. 12. A systematic review of the impact of US firearms legislation on suicide rates found some studies showing a reduction in suicide rates, but the findings were inconsistent (Hahn 2005). 13. Sharp objects are involved in only a small proportion of suicides, accounting for 2.5% in Japan and 2% in Australia (WHO 2009). However, self-cutting is a common form of deliberate self-harm. 14. Legislation can be used to limit access to sharp objects. For example, in the United Kingdom, it is an offense to carry a knife or other sharp object in public without a valid reason. 15. In England and Wales, motor vehicle exhaust-related deaths peaked in the early 1990s. In 1993, legislation required all new petrol vehicles to be fitted with catalytic converters, which reduce carbon monoxide emissions. 16. Suicide deaths by motor vehicle exhaust subsequently declined throughout the 1990s (Brock 2003). 17. In the USA, rates of motor vehicle-related carbon monoxide deaths declined from 10.0 to 4.9 per million person-years between 1968 and 1998 (Mott 2002). This decline was associated with the enforcement of automobile emissions standards set by the 1970 Clean Air Act, with the first catalytic converters introduced in 1975. 18. Suicide by drowning accounts for 1% of suicides in the USA and 15–20% in Ireland (Lunetta 2014). Drowning is a highly accessible method of suicide, particularly in areas with easy access to bodies of water. 19. Determining whether a drowning death is due to suicide or accidental causes can be challenging (Haw 2016). 20. Continuous surveillance and the construction of barriers on bridges could reduce the number of suicides by drowning. 21. Suicide by charcoal burning has emerged as a new method of suicide, particularly in Asian societies (Pan 2010). 22. A recent study found that limiting access to charcoal in major retail outlets was effective in reducing the rate of suicide by charcoal burning (Yip 2010). 23. Most suicides by jumping occur from high-rise residential buildings (Beautrais 2007). Other common sites include bridges, cliffs, and terraces. 24. Studies have demonstrated that constructing barriers and fencing at high-risk jumping sites, especially bridges, can lead to a reduction in the number of deaths (Beautrais 2001; Bennewith 2007; Cox 2013; Pelletier 2007; Pirkis 2013; Pirkis 2015). 25. Suicide by collision with a train is a highly lethal method of death and accounts for 1–12% of suicides internationally (Krysinska 2008; van Houwelingen 2010). 26. A study evaluating the effectiveness of installing platform screen doors as a means of preventing railway suicides found a significant reduction in railway suicides following the installation of such barriers (Law 2009). 27. Restricting public access to railway tracks can be achieved through legislation and the installation of surveillance devices. 28. In the 1970s, a reduction in the prescribing of barbiturates was associated with a subsequent decline in suicides resulting from barbiturate poisoning (Carlsten 1996). 29. Legislation on the packaging of paracetamol and salicylates was introduced in the UK in September 1998, restricting the number of tablets that could be sold in a single transaction. 30. Some evidence suggests that this legislation led to a reduction in the number of tablets taken in overdose cases (Hawton 2001), although some authors dispute this finding (Morgan 2007).
